author: Miles_Brundage
text: There are exceptions! But I suspect that some are worried about buying, or being seen as buying, big tech's hype on AI, and that this skews them towards making stronger statements re: what AI will never do, won't do anytime soon, etc. than they'd otherwise make.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Final example: the economic impacts of AI. I suspect some on the left are not as inclined to take radical economic disruption as a serious possibility, vs. what you'd expect from their commitments to the interests of those who could be negatively affected in such scenarios.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: The NSCAI report, for example, talks about AGI as if it's a serious (albeit long term) possibility--something you'd be hard pressed to find in the work of many who focus on the social justice dimensions of AI.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: There are various reasons for this, but this may be in part because some of the chief concerns of the "AI and national security" crowd such as great power racing/conflict presume a certain level of "optimism" about AI progress that isn't always shared by more left leaning folks.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Consider also the intersection of AI and national security. To put things crudely, one might say that compared to those working on domestic FR issues, those who work on the international + military dimensions of AI tend to be more conservative and friendly to big tech.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: (There are lots of reasons to be skeptical of FR that still hold even given hypothetically "perfect" performance, so this critique definitely doesn't apply to everyone, and I'm not saying it was even the wrong initial focus. I'm just trying to illustrate a class of failure modes)

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Take face recognition for example. A lot of activism related to face recognition has focused on arguing for restrictions based on ways in which FR works badly today. It's true FR has limitations of robustness/bias but this is not a future proof basis for opposition.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Still, I'd love to see less correlation here. We're at risk of people talking past each other just when dialogue is most important, and of people self-selecting into working on different problems alongside people with the same ideologies, and making worse policy as a result.

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
That's not to say that the hypey perspective is always the correct one. These are hard questions with some irreducible uncertainty. 

And there are some risks to overestimating progress (personally I think they're smaller than underestimating it but that's another thread!).

author: Miles_Brundage
text: So, who cares if there were a correlation/causal link here and why bother tweeting about it? I care because managing AI's societal impacts is hard, and it will be even harder if people disagree not just about how to weigh values in a particular context but on the basic facts.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: For example, something can be human-like in its performance while still having "cheated" in how it got there (e.g. consuming more data than humans ever could). Or something can be of massive economic significance without contributing much to scientific understanding.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: 3. One can interpret impressiveness of AI progress in a lot of different ways, and not all of them require conceding much ground/originality/brilliance etc. to those who work in AI. Things can be impressive in one way without being impressive in other ways.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: So one can consistently think that a capability is important, impressive, world-changing, human-like, etc. without necessarily bestowing all or even much of the ultimate credit to those directly involved. Again, not saying this is always the right framing but that it's coherent.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Indeed, AI research draws heavily from concepts and findings that first originated in academia. Most of the citations in any given paper will usually be to outside authors, and likewise, people rely on a large ecosystem of software tools.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: 2. Even if one focuses exclusively on the algorithmic and engineering sides of things, here again it is reasonable to distribute credit more widely than just the individuals/organizations directly involved in an AI project/system.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: (I'm not necessarily endorsing the strongest form of the above framing, and IMO credit varies a lot across AI projects/domains. The point is just that this is a perfectly coherent framing, and consistent with left leaning politics and tech company skepticism)

author: Miles_Brundage
text: If one adopts a more data-/hardware-centric view of AI progress, one can view AI capabilities as being amazing and impactful, but still giving the credit mostly to civilization as a whole (through global hardware supply chains, widespread contributions to Internet data, etc.).

author: Miles_Brundage
text: 1. "X did Y" usually implies "X deserves full or substantial credit for Y." But one need not believe that those who build AI systems deserve full credit for their impressiveness. AI progress is driven not just by new algorithms and engineering but computing hardware and data.

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
It's understandable that one might see these as having some inherent link--if X did Y, and Y is impressive, doesn't that imply X did something impressive? 

There are at least three reasons why this framing doesn't necessarily apply to AI progress, though.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: To be more precise, I think there is a strong correlation in AI ethics/policy world between (A) thinking that present/past AI achievements are overhyped and future progress is likely to be slow, and (B) left leaning political views and skepticism re: big tech companies/elites.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: (The premise is admittedly speculative--I am confident there's a correlation but less so re: causality. Best theory I have but will be curious for reactions. There are of course other reasons to be unimpressed such as things really being unimpressive, fear of seeming naive, etc.)

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
I think some are reticent to be impressed by AI progress partly because they associate that with views they don't like--e.g. that tech co's are great or tech ppl are brilliant. 

But these are not nec related. It'd be better if views on AI were less correlated with other stuff.🧵

text: Hopefully this entices more folks to read the full paper, which I couldn’t do justice to here. Look forward to hearing what people think of our work!!

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Overall I hope the paper answers many of folks’ current Qs and some they didn’t know they should be asking, and sparks more. We also wanted to pair all this work with the debut of the capability details to reinforce a norm of frontloading detailed impact investigations in AI.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: There’s a lot more in the paper! Didn’t try to cover it all as others will share their own takes, and I’ll RT/link to those as they come out.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: We also explore the economic implications of code generating LMs. While model limitations and the multifaceted nature of programming/engineering roles mean the effect will prob. not be massive overnight, we expect it to grow w/ capabilities. We map many topics for further work.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: On alignment with user intent, we find code LMs do not by default “try” to produce the best possible code and are responsive to the details of provided context. Along the way we introduce a contextually appropriate definition of misalignment + identify many areas for improvement.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: We think the limited system-level design capabilities of current models + stuff like rate limiting will help limit malicious use risk but there are many areas for further exploration/vigilance as models improve + diffuse. Also opportunities for e.g. proactive bug finding!

author: Miles_Brundage
text: We also explore the security implications of code generation. We make more rigorous versions of some points that have been discussed a bit in social media (e.g. possible introduction of bugs) and also carefully explore the malicious uses towards which these models could be put.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Note that we focus on research models in a “raw” setting so these kinds of findings are sort of an upper bound on bias in production—various mitigations are possible + people typically think about specs to some extent vs just writing code ASAP—but more work is still needed.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: A related issue is bias: here again there is some amount of “more of the same” re: problematic language being possible to produce, though more interestingly we shed light on ways language models could—more literally—encode biases via program design.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: As with prior LMs, reliability and robustness are below the level at which one could trust these systems to operate autonomously safely in many contexts. We discuss related issues like sandboxed experimentation, human oversight, and failure modes like bad security habits.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Language models trained specifically on code “inherit” some of the same societal issues as those trained on natural language, but we also break a lot of new ground in exploring novel failure modes + misuse risks.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: We only touch briefly on the upsides since these are more obvious and “automatic” (requiring less active effort to address) than the risks, but these include making coding more accessible, increasing productivity/code quality, and making new types of software possible.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: So, what do we actually find? A lot of things, hence the relevant sections taking up much of the paper and many appendices, but I’ll highlight a few tidbits.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: One quick framing point is that this is a paper on a set of research-oriented early Codex models, not GitHub Copilot as a product or the related production models, though the paper does give a flavor for the work that went into the latter + I think many points will generalize.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: The societal impacts stuff was again a huge collaborative effort in and of itself. @HeidyKhlaaf @GretchenMarina @GirishSastry @PamelaMishkin @BethMayBarnes @Adversariel Matt Knight mapped the risks, ran experiments, identified key open Qs etc., and more provided advice/feedback.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: I’ll have more to say on the societal implication stuff than the capabilities + eval thereof, but will briefly note the many fascinating and hard-won results including the effectiveness of sampling many times + how this relates to temperature, novel eval dataset + framework, etc.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: First, just want to emphasize how collaborative the effort has been. Assessing the societal implications of any technology—especially pre-widespread deployment—is inherently hard and requires drawing on lots of disciplinary perspectives. See long authors list + acknowledgements!

author: Miles_Brundage
text: P.S. to be super clear, this is far from the only issue in AI policy today, and not nec. the biggest - there's also good/timely work that isn't acted on, collective action problems, etc. - and lots of publications are actionable. Just something that's been on my mind lately.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: @kaixhin @jesswhittles @MaCroPhilosophy I do (and feel bad for flaking on feedback 😬). That's exciting, and indeed in the sweet spot IMO.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: But I feel like there's probably room for Pareto improvements here, e.g. opportunities for impact for independent/academic actors that don't require their being captured, and opportunities for improved decision-making by industry/government. Curious for others' thoughts!

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Again, not everyone has the same theory of change/impact, and it's reasonable for people to produce some amount of "proof of work" publications + other work I/industry/governments don't find useful. And there are big structural issues at play.

So it would have been great to see lots of effort to develop detailed policy proposals for what OSTP, NSF, etc. should do on AI under the Biden administration, with big announcements on this in Dec./Jan. This mostly didn't happen, which feels like a missed opportunity.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: The AI policy community, for the most part, failed to systematically prepare for the change of administration that just happened. More mature policy communities like defense/energy/cyber etc. know that a change of administration is a key opportunity and prepare accordingly.

So I think to some extent, this just a structurally difficult problem. But nevertheless, I think more could be done to increase the impact of AI policy work by taking into account technical/political timing. Take the Biden administration, for example.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Another factor is that many decisions that need to be made on AI are super detailed, e.g. for GPT-3, OpenAI has to make decisions re: many specific applications that were hard to anticipate in advance. And it's easier to influence those "from the inside" at the time they arise.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: There are valuable proofs of concept re: e.g. safety/bias measures at small scale in academia that are picked up on by industry and I've seen instances of that. But industry also sometimes is preoccupied with things that specifically arise at scale, e.g. few-shot learning in LMs.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Another contributing factor happening in parallel: access to resources. It's hard, as an independent/academic actor, to do work that is directly applicable to the large-scale systems built in industry, without large-scale resources (e.g. data/compute).

author: Miles_Brundage
text: So there can be good reasons to work on things outside the sweet spot, but there should nevertheless probably be more work that is in the sweet spot IMO. It's bad that e.g. lots of decision-making on language models right now is not super informed by independent/academic work.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Not everyone sees impact this way, e.g. they have a "thing" (research agenda/lens) and don't want to pivot, or they focus on more timeless topics, or they don't want to be (seen as) captured by industry w.r.t what they work on, or they want past decisions to be overturned, etc.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: In order to hit that sweet spot, you may need to be in orgs making key decisions, or be in touch with them, or specifically *try* to do work in the sweet spot, e.g. picking up on trends in the literature and jumping on them quickly. Many researchers aren't in these categories.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: That is, by default, people miss the sweet spot between when AI outcomes are not yet foreseeable in detail, and when a lot of the key decisions have been made. That time period is short (small number of months/years), e.g. I think language models are in the sweet spot right now.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: What's going on here besides people optimizing for different things, or not bothering to do their homework? One answer is that AI policy researchers are falling victim to Collingridge's dilemma (https://t.co/0WsNnBQDal).

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Now, not everyone is striving for novelty or informing the decision-making of industry, academic researchers, or governments. People are also often trying to make a name for themselves, or to put pressure on certain actors, etc.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: ...but even a lot of that work is quickly forgotten by readers (or at least me), especially if it's overly abstract and not really connected to any actual decisions that need to be made (by researchers, industry, government, consumers, or others).

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
...so to an extent, the AI "ethics-washing" concern is valid. That's part of the story here.

But that's not the only failure happening. There's also well-intentioned research that "checks the boxes" of novelty (i.e. cites prior work, makes some novel conceptual contribution)...

author: Miles_Brundage
text: I think there can be value in saying things that others have said, if they are accompanied by concrete/falsifiable commitments, or are surprising given the speaker. But often it seems like there's just been little effort to even try to say anything new, falsifiable, or credible.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Perhaps the largest growth sector has been the "gray literature." Not peer-viewed papers, and not authoritative government policies...but blog posts and "report" PDFs from academics/companies/non-profits/governments. These often seem intended to show "proof of work" on AI policy.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: AI policy publications come in various forms, including peer-reviewed academic papers, government reports, corporate blog posts, working group/committee outputs, "AI principles," etc.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: By any reasonable measure, there are vastly more publications on AI policy than there was, say, 5 years ago. This has roughly paralleled the growth in AI capabilities research, applications, and regulation over that time period.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: [A note on terminology: AI ethics/policy/safety/governance etc. can be distinguished in various ways. I use "AI policy" as a catch-all for all these here because I think my points are pretty general, but I'm interested in feedback on that among other points made here!]
